questions.question: Q1. A LiPo pack is labelled 4S 1500 mAh, 100C continuous. What continuous current can it legally supply?

explanations.a: Incorrect — 100 is the C-rating, not a current. It has to be multiplied by the capacity in amp-hours.
explanations.b: Correct — I_cont = C_cont x Capacity_Ah = 100 x 1.5 Ah = 150 A.
explanations.c: Incorrect — this multiplies the C-rating by the capacity in milliamp-hours instead of amp-hours.
explanations.d: Incorrect — this is unrelated to the discharge rating.

questions.question: Q2. What does the S number in a 4S LiPo pack describe?

answers.a: The number of cells wired in series, which sets the pack voltage
answers.c: The number of cells wired in parallel, which sets the capacity
answers.d: The number of balance leads on the connector

explanations.a: Correct — four cells in series give roughly 14.8 V nominal and 16.8 V fully charged.
explanations.b: Incorrect — that is the C-rating, quoted separately.
explanations.c: Incorrect — parallel cells are denoted P, and they add capacity rather than voltage.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the balance lead count follows from the cell count, but it is not what S means.

questions.question: Q3. Two 4S packs are offered: 5200 mAh at 30C, and 1500 mAh at 100C. Which can safely supply the larger continuous current?

answers.a: The 5200 mAh pack, because capacity and current capability are the same thing
answers.b: The 1500 mAh pack, at 150 A against the 5200 mAh pack's 156 A
answers.c: The 5200 mAh pack, at 156 A against the 1500 mAh pack's 150 A
answers.d: They are identical, because both are 4S

explanations.a: Incorrect — capacity and discharge capability are separate specifications entirely.
explanations.b: Incorrect — the arithmetic is right for the 1500 mAh pack, but it is the smaller of the two limits.
explanations.c: Correct — 5.2 Ah x 30C = 156 A against 1.5 Ah x 100C = 150 A. The two are nearly equal despite a threefold capacity difference, which is exactly why the mAh label alone tells you nothing about current capability.
explanations.d: Incorrect — cell count sets voltage, not current capability.

questions.question: Q4. Why does a pack's terminal voltage fall as soon as a heavy load is applied?

answers.a: The cells lose charge instantly at high current
answers.b: Current through the pack's internal resistance drops voltage inside the pack itself
answers.c: The ESC reduces the voltage to protect the motor
answers.d: The nominal voltage rating only applies at zero current

explanations.a: Incorrect — the sag appears the instant load is applied, long before meaningful charge has been drawn.
explanations.b: Correct — V_terminal = N_cells x (V_oc - I x R_cell,eff). The I x R term is lost across the cells' own resistance.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the ESC switches the pack voltage through to the motor; it does not regulate it down.
explanations.d: Incorrect — nominal voltage is a chemistry convention, not a no-load-only specification.

questions.question: Q5. Which cell property most directly limits how high a pack's C-rating can be?

answers.a: The internal resistance of the cells
answers.b: The physical size of the discharge connector

explanations.a: Correct — internal resistance sets both the heat generated at a given current and the voltage sag, and it is what caps the safe continuous rate.
explanations.b: Incorrect — connectors are chosen to suit the pack, not the other way round.
explanations.c: Incorrect — balance leads are for charging, not for discharge capability.
explanations.d: Incorrect — capacity and discharge rate are independent; a small high-C pack beats a large low-C one on current.

questions.question: Q6. In the simulator, what is the loaded cell voltage below which the bench reports an ESC brownout?

explanations.a: Incorrect — 3.70 V is roughly the nominal resting voltage of a LiPo cell, not the brownout limit.
explanations.b: Incorrect — 2.80 V per cell is deep into damage territory, well past the point where the ESC has already dropped out.
explanations.c: Correct — the bench flags ESC brownout when loaded voltage sags below 3.30 V per cell.
explanations.d: Incorrect — 4.20 V per cell is the fully charged voltage, the top of the range rather than the floor.

questions.question: Q7. The open-circuit voltage of a cell follows V_oc = 3.50 + 0.70(SoC) + 0.10(SoC)^3. What does the shape of that curve imply for a voltage-based fuel gauge?

answers.a: Voltage maps linearly onto state of charge, so a simple gauge is accurate
answers.b: The curve is steep at both ends and flat through the middle, so voltage is a poor indicator of charge over most of the discharge
answers.c: Voltage stays constant until the pack is empty, then collapses
answers.d: The cubic term dominates, so voltage rises as the pack empties

explanations.a: Incorrect — the cubic term exists precisely because the relationship is not linear.
explanations.b: Correct — the flat middle region means a large change in charge produces very little change in voltage, so a voltage-only gauge has its worst resolution exactly where most of the flight happens.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the voltage falls continuously; it is the rate of fall that varies.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the cubic coefficient is small and positive, so voltage falls monotonically as SoC falls.

questions.question: Q8. A brief current spike occurs as the throttle ramps up. Why does the bench not immediately flag a fault?

answers.a: Spikes are ignored entirely by the instrumentation
answers.b: The fault timer requires roughly three seconds of sustained draw above the continuous limit
answers.c: The C-rating only applies below 50% throttle
answers.d: The pack automatically raises its C-rating during transients

explanations.a: Incorrect — the spike is measured and displayed; it simply does not by itself constitute a fault.
explanations.b: Correct — packs tolerate short bursts above the continuous rating, so the bench only latches a vent fault after about three seconds of sustained over-current.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the continuous rating applies at every throttle setting.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the burst rating is a separate published figure, not something the pack generates on demand.

questions.question: Q9. Why does doubling a pack's capacity fail to double hover endurance?

answers.a: The larger pack's own mass has to be lifted too, so hover current rises with it
answers.b: Larger packs always have lower C-ratings
answers.c: The ESC limits current more aggressively on larger packs
answers.d: Capacity has no effect on endurance at all

explanations.a: Correct — endurance is capacity divided by hover current, and adding cells raises both. The gain flattens out and eventually reverses.
explanations.b: Incorrect — often true in practice, but not the reason the endurance curve bends over.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the current limit is a property of the ESC, not of the pack size.
explanations.d: Incorrect — capacity clearly extends endurance, just not proportionally.

questions.question: Q10. What does a coulomb counter measure when it estimates state of charge?

answers.a: The pack's terminal voltage at each instant
answers.b: The integral of current over time, that is, charge drawn out of the pack
answers.c: The internal resistance of each cell
answers.d: The pack's temperature rise during discharge

explanations.a: Incorrect — that describes a voltage-based gauge, a different and less accurate method.
explanations.b: Correct — it accumulates amp-hours drawn and subtracts them from an assumed total capacity.
explanations.c: Incorrect — internal resistance affects sag but is not what a coulomb counter integrates.
explanations.d: Incorrect — temperature is a symptom of losses, not a measure of charge.
